Le survivant d’un massacre témoigne cont: Massacre survivor testifies against former soldier who found refuge in Canada
Un survivant du massacre de Las Dos Erre: A survivor of the Las Dos Erres massacre and a former lieutenant accused of taking part in it both live in Canada. The survivor speaks out.
Ramiro Osorio Cristales dans le hall de: Ramiro Osorio Cristales in the lobby of the Federal Court of Canada in Ottawa, after testifying before the judge. Photo: Loubna Chlaikhy
Quand on est journaliste, on rencontre d: As a journalist, you meet many people who have lived through all kinds of joyful and painful events, and who trust you with their stories. Ramiro Osorio Cristales’s is in a class of its own. I met a man who has endured trauma so severe that words seem inadequate to describe it. He is one of the few survivors of the Las Dos Erres massacre, carried out in Guatemala in 1982.
Il y a plus d’une décennie, il découvre: More than a decade ago, he discovered that one of the men who tormented his family was also living in Canada… A real shock. On November 15, he testified before the Federal Court, which must decide whether to strip the war criminal of his citizenship. I travelled to Ottawa to attend the hearing and meet Ramiro Osorio Cristales. The gentleness in his eyes hides an extraordinary capacity for resilience. I want to thank him for sharing his story with such simplicity.
Cet article décrit des faits qui peuvent: This article describes events that some readers may find disturbing. Also, to avoid putting the witness in danger, I have not included any details about his current personal life (where he lives, what he does for work, etc.).
Merci pour votre soutien et bonne lectur: Thank you for your support, and happy reading!
<strong>La Cour fédérale du Canada étudi: The Federal Court of Canada is hearing a case unlike any other. It must rule on whether to revoke the Canadian citizenship of Jorge Vinicio Sosa Orantes. He is accused of being one of the war criminals allegedly responsible for the Las Dos Erres massacre, committed in Guatemala in 1982. On the witness stand, one of only three survivors of that tragedy, Ramiro Osorio Cristales, tells his story. He too found refuge in Canada. Report.
« Quand je me suis réveillé, il y avait: “When I woke up, there were two other children with me. We got up and saw the bodies, bodies everywhere. We went out of the church, and I saw other bodies hanging from the trees.” Facing Justice Roger R. Lafrenière of the Federal Court of Canada, his voice trembling, Ramiro Osorio Cristales keeps his head high. For more than two hours, he recounts the night of December 7, 1982, when more than 200 residents of his native village, Las Dos Erres, were killed by the Guatemalan army during a bloody civil war. He was five years old, and he is one of only three survivors.
Devenu orphelin, Ramiro Osorio Cristales: Orphaned, Ramiro Osorio Cristales had no choice but to grow up in the family of one of the soldiers accused of being responsible for the massacre. It was only at the age of 18 that he managed to flee his country and find refuge in Canada, where he was granted political asylum in 2005.
En 2011, celui qui vient de devenir père: In 2011, having just become a father for the first time, he discovered that another man suspected of taking part in the massacre had taken refuge in Canada: Jorge Vinicio Sosa Orantes. A former second lieutenant in the Guatemalan army, he is accused of leading the Kaibiles special unit that tortured, raped and executed the villagers.
De 1960 à 1996, le Guatemala a connu une: From 1960 to 1996, Guatemala was engulfed in a civil war that pitted the military against guerilleros. In the spring of 1982, General Efrain Rios Montt took power in a coup and launched a violent campaign of repression against the guerrillas. A special forces unit known as the “Kaibiles” was deployed to fight the rebels.
Plus de 42 ans après la journée qui a fa: More than 42 years after the day that made Ramiro Osorio Cristales an orphan, the Federal Court is examining the proceedings to revoke Mr. Sosa Orantes’s citizenship, launched by the Canadian government in 2017. It is in this context that Mr. Cristales was heard by the Canadian justice system as a witness on November 15. Although Jorge Vinicio Sosa Orantes is not being tried for the crimes he is accused of committing in Guatemala, the federal judge is hearing testimony and evidence that would show his involvement and justify stripping him of his citizenship. The former soldier was not present at the hearing.
Depuis plus d’une décennie, il mène un c: For more than a decade, he has been fighting, with the help of Lawyers Without Borders Canada (LWBC), to have Mr. Sosa Orantes brought to justice for the war crimes he is accused of committing in Guatemala.
‍<strong>« Je pensais être en sécurité d: “I thought I was safe in my adopted country”
Comment un homme accusé de crimes de gue: How can a man accused of war crimes live out his old age in peace in Canada? To understand, we have to go back a few decades, to when Mr. Sosa Orantes left Guatemala for the United States. Arriving in San Francisco in May 1985, he applied for political asylum for himself and his family, without success.
Jorge Vinicio Sosa Orantes poursuit son: Jorge Vinicio Sosa Orantes continued his journey farther north, to Canada. Here, his asylum claim was accepted and he obtained citizenship in 1992. According to Lawyers Without Borders, he also managed to obtain American citizenship in 2008. For two decades, he lived like any other Canadian citizen. According to investigations by ProPublica, the man accused of being a war criminal reportedly bought a house, ran karate schools and travelled around the world.
« Quand j’ai découvert, grâce à Avocats: “When I found out, thanks to Lawyers Without Borders, that he was living in Canada – and that he was here even before I arrived as a refugee – it was a shock. I was very surprised and a little frightened too, because I thought I was safe in my adopted country. But that wasn’t the case,” says Mr. Cristales. Supported by the association of lawyers, which provides him with pro bono legal assistance, he has been asking the Canadian justice system since 2010 to arrest Jorge Vinicio Sosa Orantes and bring him to trial.
Ce n’est que le 18 janvier 2011 que l’an: It was not until January 18, 2011, that the former officer was arrested by Canadian authorities. The decision followed an extradition request from the United States, where he is accused of lying on his citizenship application. Mr. Sosa Orantes was extradited on September 21, 2012, after a ruling by the Alberta Court of Appeal, in the province where he lived.
« Je sais qu’il doit être assez vieux au: “I know he must be quite old now, but he was trained to kill people.” - Ramiro Osorio Cristales, survivor of the Las Dos Erres massacre
Déçu, mais décidé à tout faire pour que: Disappointed but determined to do everything he could to make the man he considers the tormentor of his family pay for his crimes, Ramiro Osorio Cristales travelled to the United States. “I testified at his trial, and the judge decided to strip him of his American citizenship and send him to prison. But that was only for lying in his administrative dealings with Immigration, not for what he did in Guatemala,” explains the man in his forties. Indeed, in the United States, “the law does not provide for extraterritorial jurisdiction over crimes against humanity,” says Lawyers Without Borders.
Il est donc condamné à une peine de 10 a: He was therefore sentenced to 10 years in prison for making false statements in an immigration proceeding and for unlawfully obtaining American citizenship.
D’après les archives judiciaires américa: According to U.S. court records, he was granted early release in July 2019 but was kept in detention by immigration authorities until early 2021.
Pour M. Cristales, le cauchemar recommen: For Mr. Cristales, the nightmare began again. He knows that Mr. Sosa Orantes is back in Canada and is free. “It’s very hard for me and for my family. We can’t help but be worried, because we don’t know where he is right now or what he plans to do. I know he must be quite old now, but he was trained to kill people,” he says, his throat tight. To protect him, this article therefore contains no details about his current life.
<strong>« J’ai le devoir de témoigner po: “I have a duty to testify for everyone who died that day”
Derrière la tendresse du bleu des yeux d: Behind the tender blue of Ramiro Osorio Cristales’s eyes, one can sense determination and fighting spirit, despite the fear, despite the trauma of having to tell once again the story of the day that marked him forever. He is one of the main witnesses heard in this exceptional trial at the Federal Court of Canada in Ottawa. “I feel the fear of speaking, but also the freedom of being a survivor who saw what happened. I have a duty to testify for everyone who died that day. I am their voice,” he says.
Dans la salle d’audience entièrement rec: In the courtroom, entirely covered in wood panelling, a few rays of winter sun make their way through narrow, tall windows. Facing the imposing bench of the federal judge, which towers over the room, Ramiro Osorio Cristales can hardly hide his nervousness. Seated in the place reserved for witnesses and victims, he faces a switched-off microphone, waiting to be given the floor.
Le magistrat rappelle laconiquement le c: The judge tersely recalls the context of this November 15, 2024, hearing, more than 13 years after the survivor’s first requests and 7 years after the government began proceedings against the accused. In the room, not a sound is heard. About ten people listen attentively from the benches reserved for the public. “We are friends of Ramiro, also from Guatemala. I came with my brothers to support him, because what he is doing is very brave and very difficult,” says a Gatineau resident during a short recess called by the judge.
À son retour, le magistrat commence son: When he returns, the judge begins his questioning: first a few general questions, then he asks Ramiro Osorio Cristales where he was when the soldiers arrived in his village on December 7, 1982. Mr. Cristales sits up straight, moves closer to the microphone and launches into a terrible account.
« Des hommes sont arrivés la nuit et ont: “Men arrived at night and knocked on our door. They started to break down the door and it woke us up. They shouted that we had to open up right away, or they would force it down. My father opened it and they hit him,” he describes calmly. The family was then escorted by armed men to the centre of the small village, located in Petén, Guatemala’s northernmost department. There, his family was split in two: his father and older brother were taken to the school, while his mother and the rest of his siblings ended up in the church with other villagers.
« L’un d’eux a attrapé ma mère, poursuit: “One of them grabbed my mother,” he continues. “I clung to her, I was crying, I begged them not to hurt her, but another one knocked her down and dragged her outside by her hair while someone else pulled me away from her.” - Ramiro Osorio Cristales, survivor of the Las Dos Erres massacre
En réalité, les militaires sont à la rec: In reality, the soldiers were looking for weapons stolen by rebels. “On December 7, 1982, the special patrol (Kaibiles, editor’s note) entered Dos Erres with the support of about 40 additional soldiers, who formed a security perimeter around the village so that no one could enter or escape,” the Attorney General of the United States wrote in his findings during Mr. Sosa Orantes’s trial in 2014.
« Je ne comprenais pas ce qu’il se passa: “I didn’t understand what was happening. People were hurt, and we could hear screams coming from the school,” he recalls. “A soldier told us: ‘If you know how to pray, do it, because no one is coming to save you.’” In a matter of seconds, the place of worship turned into hell. The soldiers tore children from their mothers and beat women; cries of pain rang out, tears flowed. “One of them grabbed my mother,” he continues. “I clung to her, I was crying, I begged them not to hurt her, but another one knocked her down and dragged her outside by her hair while someone else pulled me away from her.”
À l’extérieur, « femmes et petites fille: Outside, “women and little girls were raped,” while “children were thrown alive into the village well.” “Members of the special patrol searched every house looking for weapons, forced villagers out of their homes and separated the women and children from the men. No weapons were found, and the villagers put up no resistance,” the U.S. Attorney General noted in 2014.
Des heures durant, Ramiro Osorio Cristal: For hours, Ramiro Osorio Cristales, who was just a five-year-old boy, hid under a pew in the church. Despite the screams of horror reaching him from outside and the fear knotting his stomach, he eventually fell asleep there, exhausted from crying.
<strong>Adopté par l’un des militaires a: Adopted by one of the soldiers accused of taking part in the massacre
« Quand je me suis réveillé, il y avait: “When I woke up, there were two other children with me. We got up and saw the bodies, bodies everywhere. We went out of the church, and I saw other bodies hanging from the trees. Everyone was dead…” says Ramiro Osorio Cristales in a whisper, his glasses fogged by the tears rolling down his cheeks. The judge offers him time to collect himself, while his lawyer hands him a box of tissues. He quickly wipes his cheeks, breathes in and continues: “The soldiers saw us, they told us to follow them. We ended up in the jungle. We walked for two days, and a military helicopter came to get us.”
Sans le savoir, il se retrouve au cœur d: Without knowing it, he found himself in the middle of a Kaibiles training centre. The Kaibiles are a special operations unit of the Guatemalan army, known for their jungle combat tactics. “We didn’t know where we were. The soldiers called this place infierno, which means hell in Spanish. They shaved our heads and gave us uniforms. I had no idea where I was,” he says.
L’enfant devient une « sorte de mascotte: The child became a “sort of mascot” for the soldiers. One of them, the one who had pulled him from his mother, decided to take him home. “He adopted me and I grew up in his house, with his family. For years, I had to live with one of the men responsible for the death of my entire family – it was horrible... I often cried and said I missed my mother, but I wasn’t allowed to talk about it. He was a very violent man…” he says, his voice catching.
Ce n’est qu’à l’âge de 18 ans qu’il parv: It was only at the age of 18 that he managed to escape that family by joining the army. But some people discovered that he was one of the survivors of the Las Dos Erres massacre and feared he would talk. His life was therefore in danger. “I applied for asylum in the United States and another in Canada. Canada was the first to say yes,” he recalls.
Livré à lui-même, il laisse tout derrièr: Left to fend for himself, he left everything behind and landed in the middle of winter in a country where he spoke neither of the languages. “Today, I can say my life is easier, not like before. Before, I had no family, I didn’t really care about my life, but now I do. I care because I have a family, a wife and children who support me,” he says on a note of hope.
Après un long chemin, Ramiro Osorio Cris: After a long journey, Ramiro Osorio Cristales seems to have managed to give his life “a meaning again,” despite the fear he has felt since learning that one of the men accused of being responsible for his trauma lives in Canada.
« Ce que je veux, c’est que la justice c: “What I want is for Canadian justice to try him for the crimes he committed in Guatemala. Taking away his citizenship is a good thing, but it’s not enough,” says Mr. Cristales, standing between two of the marble columns in the grand lobby of the Federal Court. It is the request he has been making for more than 13 years with the help of Lawyers Without Borders Canada.
En 2012, lorsque le Canada a pris la déc: In 2012, when Canada decided to extradite Mr. Sosa Orantes to the United States, it had the opportunity to send the criminal back to his country of origin. At the time, Guatemala had in fact requested his extradition for acts amounting to crimes against humanity, without success. The massacre survivors’ quest for justice has therefore still not been heard.
En mai 2022, Avocats sans frontières Can: In May 2022, Lawyers Without Borders Canada and Ramiro Osorio Cristales travelled to Ottawa in hopes of meeting David Lametti, then Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada. “The door was closed,” the non-profit organization says. Today, Mr. Cristales hopes that Jorge Vinicio Sosa Orantes will be stripped of his Canadian citizenship. However, he hopes it will be only Canada’s first action against this man, and not the end point of his efforts.
« En vertu du principe de la compétence: “Under the principle of universal jurisdiction, the Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act gives the Canadian government the power to bring criminal proceedings against Mr. Sosa Orantes,” Lawyers Without Borders Canada points out. “Universal jurisdiction can be used for the most serious crimes committed in another country, as with the Las Dos Erres massacre. The person suspected of the crime must be present in Canada,” the organization continues. It is handling this case in collaboration with the Canadian Partnership for International Justice (CPIJ).
Si le Canada dispose des outils juridiqu: While Canada has the legal tools to bring this man to justice, a completely different obstacle could stand in the way, according to Fannie Lafontaine, a law professor at Université Laval.
« Les poursuites au Canada ne sont possi: “Prosecutions in Canada are only possible with the consent of the Attorney General of Canada, a global trend that serves to limit the negative diplomatic consequences of universal jurisdiction.” - Fannie Lafontaine, law professor
« Le succès de la Loi sur les crimes de: “The success of the War Crimes Act may depend not so much on the strength of its provisions or on judicial interpretations, but on the political will to use its full potential against international criminals found on Canadian territory,” she writes in a scholarly article titled Criminels de guerre au Canada ? La valse-hésitation historique entre poursuites et expulsions. Under the International Criminal Court (ICC) system, states do indeed have the responsibility to prosecute those responsible for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes.
« Les poursuites au Canada ne sont possi: “Prosecutions in Canada are only possible with the consent of the Attorney General of Canada, a global trend that serves to limit the negative diplomatic consequences of universal jurisdiction, but that risks sacrificing justice and the rule of law on the altar of political and economic considerations,” she explains. The expert stresses that while Canada’s political leadership certainly has the ability to prosecute Mr. Sosa Orantes, it must also have the will to do so.
On sait toutefois qu’il existe un fossé: However, we know there is a considerable gap between the promise of international justice based on ICC rules, as with the principle of universal jurisdiction enshrined in Canadian law, and the reality of its enforcement. “Over the past two years, Lawyers Without Borders Canada, together with the Canadian Partnership for International Justice, has repeatedly reminded the Canadian government of the powers it has. These appeals have gone unanswered,” laments the organization, which continues to call for legal proceedings in Canada over the war crimes Mr. Sosa Orantes is accused of committing in Guatemala.
La récente émission d’un mandat d’arrêt: The recent issuance of an international arrest warrant against Benjamin Netanyahu is a more recent example of the challenges surrounding the application of international law. Since the ICC announced it, some countries have hesitated to state that they would arrest the Israeli prime minister if he set foot on their territory.
De son côté, le premier ministre Justin: For his part, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau has suggested that he would enforce the international arrest warrant. “Canada is one of the founders of our international legal systems, and we will always follow the decisions and rulings of these bodies,” he said on November 21 at a press conference in Toronto.
Ramiro Osorio Cristales et les personnes: Ramiro Osorio Cristales and those who support him hope that this reaffirmation of Canada’s commitment to international law will help advance their cause. “This commitment, which is welcome, should also translate into an unequivocal refusal to allow Canadian territory to shelter individuals suspected of the most serious crimes,” they insist.
La date de rendu du jugement n’a pas enc: The Federal Court has not yet disclosed when it will hand down its ruling. The defence is to submit its conclusions this week.
